description:
🌕 We are Lunar Compass, a team of engineers, innovators, and space enthusiasts building smarter solutions for lunar exploration.

Led by Saifullah, a Computer Engineering student and ICESCO CanSat Symposium delegate, we combine expertise in AI, software, hardware, and FPGA development.

🚀 Our mission: Build an intelligent Lunar Landing Site Navigator to identify safe landing zones using terrain, slope, and crater analysis.
summary: SELENE-Nav is an interactive 3D web app that shows mission planners, educators and the public, in seconds, whether a landing site at the Moon’s South Pole will have sunlight for power and a view of Earth for direct radio contact. Users start on a full-Moon globe and fly down to real NASA LOLA terrain. They pick a landing date and mission length, then draw a landing ellipse. SELENE-Nav calculates the terrain horizon around every 80 m point in the ellipse and checks the Sun and Earth hour by hour. It reports sunlight, Earth visibility, longest darkness, slope and time until sunset or Earthset, with a clear Good, Risky or Not recommended verdict. Users can adjust the thresholds, find a better spot nearby, get the best site and date suggested automatically, and save and share plans to compare them. The Sun and Earth positions match JPL Horizons to within 0.006°. This matters because South Pole missions face extreme lighting: the Sun barely clears the horizon, and moving a few kilometres or a few days can turn a good site into a dark, silent one. When a launch slips, teams need answers fast, and SELENE-Nav makes them quick and accessible.
details:
What it does and how it works
At the Moon’s South Pole, the Sun never rises more than about 1.6 degrees above the horizon, and Earth moves up and down by about 7 degrees. Nearby mountains and crater rims can easily block both. A lander that loses the Sun loses solar power. A lander that loses sight of Earth can’t communicate directly with mission control. SELENE-Nav helps planners judge whether a landing site and date will avoid these problems.

The app opens on a 3D model of the full Moon and flies down to the South Pole, built from real NASA LOLA elevation data. The user then follows three steps:

  1. Choose a landing date and how many days the mission will last.
  2. Draw a landing ellipse on the terrain, or start from a known crater or an Artemis III candidate region.
  3. Run the analysis.

For every 80 m point inside the ellipse, SELENE-Nav calculates how high the surrounding terrain rises in every direction, out to 250 km and including the Moon’s curvature. It then compares this horizon with the Sun’s and Earth’s positions for every hour of the mission.

The result is a verdict of Good, Risky or Not recommended, with a one-sentence explanation of why. Supporting numbers include:

  • percentage of time in sunlight
  • percentage of time Earth is visible
  • usable time, when the Sun and Earth are both visible
  • longest period of darkness
  • ground slope and permanently shadowed area
  • time until sunset and Earthset after landing

A timeline slider animates sunlight and Earth visibility over the mission. Charts and a 360-degree horizon view show exactly which terrain blocks the Sun or Earth.

Benefits
A site-and-date check that would normally mean several expert tools and raw data now takes a few seconds.

  • If a site performs poorly, “Find a better spot nearby” searches within 20 km for a better location.
  • “Suggest best plan” searches the whole South Pole over up to 90 days to find the best site and landing time.
  • Users can save up to 10 plans, compare them side by side, and share them with a link.
  • Verdict thresholds can be adjusted, or set from Default, Strict and Relaxed presets, to suit different missions.

Intended impact
Missions often face hardware problems or launch delays that change the landing date. SELENE-Nav lets teams quickly see whether their site still works, or find a better one, so science and engineering teams can make decisions from the same clear information. It also helps students and the public understand why landing at the lunar South Pole is so difficult.

Tools and technologies

  • Languages: TypeScript, Python and GLSL (graphics shaders).
    • NASA LOLA South Pole terrain, slope and shadow maps
    • NASA SVS Moon data
    • NASA JPL DE440/DE421 ephemerides and JPL Horizons for Sun and Earth positions
  • Hosting: Vercel. It runs in any modern web browser with no special hardware.

Creativity

  • One smooth zoom takes the user from the whole Moon down to detailed 80 m analysis.
  • Complex geometry becomes a simple verdict with a plain-English reason.
  • The app can automatically suggest the best landing site and date.
  • Animated Sun and Earth visibility shows the user why a site works or fails.

Factors we considered

  • Scientific accuracy:
    • real terrain, lunar curvature, Earth parallax and lunar libration
    • the Sun treated as a disc rather than a point
    • Sun and Earth positions checked against NASA SVS and JPL Horizons, which agree within 0.006 degrees
  • Speed: heavy data was precomputed and the app loads in stages.
  • Ease of use: a clear step-by-step flow for non-experts, with details available for specialists.
  • Honesty: the Data & Methods panel states the app’s limits, such as 1.28 km resolution for region-wide searches and no antenna model.
